aka: Ajinomoto Build-up Film, build-up film, ABF build-up film, ABF substrate, ABF substrates
plain: The insulating film inside the substrate, the small layered board that the chips in a high-end package sit on. The board is built up in layers, and a sheet of this epoxy film, about 10 micrometers thick, separates each layer of copper wiring from the next. The Japanese food company Ajinomoto first developed it in 1999.
why: Ajinomoto told investors in June 2026 that its film has held over 95 percent of its market since its launch. The company says practically all high-performance computers and servers rely on it.

aka: AI accelerator, XPU, accelerators
plain: A chip built to do the one kind of arithmetic machine learning needs, multiplying large grids of numbers, far faster than a general-purpose processor can. Nvidia's graphics processors, Google's Tensor Processing Units and Amazon's Trainium are all accelerators.
why: The whole supply chain exists to make accelerators, and export licenses are granted or refused for them.

aka: 2.5D packaging, 3D packaging, 2.5D, 2.5D work, advanced packaging plants
plain: The steps that assemble several finished chips into one component, sitting side by side or stacked, wired together closely enough to behave like a single larger chip. Ordinary packaging only puts one chip into a protective case with contacts on the bottom.
why: A modern AI accelerator needs more circuitry than a lithography machine can print in one exposure, and its memory must sit beside the logic, so it is assembled this way. Epoch AI found that TSMC's CoWoS packaging and the memory itself were the main limits on AI chip production in 2025.

aka: atomic layer deposition
plain: A way of coating a chip a fraction of an atomic layer at a time. Each pulse of gas sticks to the surface and stops once the surface is covered. So the film comes out the same thickness on the floor and on the walls of a hole more than 50 times deeper than it is wide.
why: US regulators call atomic layer deposition an enabler of stacked memory and of FinFET and gate-all-around logic, and export rules name some of its tools directly. Chinese toolmakers held 2.6 percent of the market in 2025 on CSET's count, most of it from Piotech.

aka: application-specific integrated circuit, custom silicon, ASICs, custom accelerator, custom accelerators, custom chip, custom AI silicon, custom AI ASICs
plain: A chip designed for one company's own workload and not sold on the open market. Google's Tensor Processing Unit and Amazon's Trainium are chips of this kind. An Nvidia part sold to any customer is not.
why: A custom chip is tuned to one company's workload, but a chip sold to everyone comes with mature software and a resale market. Design houses such as Broadcom and Marvell turn the buyer's design into silicon and sell the finished chips to the buyer.

aka: automated test equipment, automatic test equipment, tester
plain: Automated test equipment, or ATE, is the machine that connects to a chip, on the wafer or in its package, feeds it test patterns and checks whether the answers coming back are right. Advantest's July 2026 investor guide counts test as the only manufacturing step that puts electrical signals through the chip.
why: An AI accelerator joins a dozen expensive pieces, and one bad piece scraps them all. So each die is tested before assembly. Advantest's April 2025 investor guide put Advantest and Teradyne at about 80 percent of the tester market.

aka: ball grid array, FC-BGA, flip-chip BGA
plain: A way of joining a packaged chip to a circuit board using a grid of small solder balls across the underside in place of a row of pins around the edge. Heating the assembly melts every ball at once into a permanent joint.
why: The number and spacing of those balls limit how much current and how many signals can reach a package.

aka: BOM
plain: The itemized list of every purchased part in a finished product and what each part cost, the way a builder's invoice prices lumber, wiring and fixtures separately.
why: A bill of materials shows which suppliers get the money a buyer spends. Epoch AI estimated in December 2025 that memory made up about half of the roughly $6,400 manufacturing cost of an Nvidia B200.

aka: Bureau of Industry and Security, part of the US Department of Commerce
plain: The US government office that decides which technologies may be exported, to whom, and on what conditions. It writes the rules, issues the licenses and brings the enforcement cases.
why: BIS wrote the US restrictions on selling AI chips and chipmaking tools to China in a series of rules. It can change a threshold by publishing a notice in the Federal Register, with no act of Congress needed.

aka: capital expenditure, capital spending
plain: Money a company spends on long-lived physical assets such as buildings, machines and servers, as distinct from salaries and other running costs.
why: The largest cloud companies' capex pays for the chips, racks and buildings of the AI buildout. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle spent $448.2 billion of capital in 2025, the sum of Epoch AI's quarterly figures. Epoch AI says they will spend $770 billion in 2026 if the trend continues.

aka: chiplets
plain: One of several smaller pieces that a chip has been deliberately split into, each manufactured separately and then wired back together inside a single package. A chip built this way is like a house assembled from prefabricated rooms.
why: Many large accelerators need more circuitry than a lithography machine can print in one exposure, so they are built from chiplets. That makes packaging, the step that joins the chiplets, the hard part. Epoch AI found that TSMC's CoWoS packaging and memory were the main limits on AI chip production in 2025.

aka: chokepoints
plain: A step in the supply chain where so few firms or countries can do the work that losing one of them stops everybody.
why: One sanction or one factory fire at a chokepoint reaches the whole industry, and so does a government policy aimed at one.

aka: complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor, complementary MOS
plain: CMOS, short for complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor, is the standard way of building digital circuits from pairs of transistors. Each n-type transistor, which switches on when the voltage on its gate is high, is matched with a p-type transistor, which switches on when that voltage is low. In either logic state one side of the circuit is off, so little current flows except while it switches.
why: CMOS became the dominant technology for making chips because its circuits drew close to zero power while idle, which kept heat in check as chips packed in more transistors. FinFET and gate-all-around transistors are newer shapes for the same n-type and p-type pairs.

aka: training compute threshold
plain: A limit set on the amount of arithmetic used to train an AI model. It counts operations, whichever chips run them. The AI Diffusion rule of January 2025 made one an export control. ECCN 4E091 covers "'Parameters' for an artificial intelligence model trained utilizing 10^26 or more 'operations'". The rules require a license to send such parameters to every destination worldwide (15 CFR 742.6(a)(13)). Article 51(2) of the EU AI Act sets Europe's line ten times lower. It presumes a model has high-impact capabilities when the cumulative computation used for training is "greater than 10^25" floating point operations.
why: Every other control threshold measures a chip, but this one measures the model the chips train. Article 51(3) of the AI Act lets the European Commission change the EU figure by delegated act. Such an act takes effect unless the European Parliament or the Council objects within three months (Article 97(6)). BIS said in May 2025 that it would not enforce the AI Diffusion rule, but 4E091 still stands in the regulations.

aka: concentration band
plain: A four-band judgment of how many firms could credibly supply a stage today, taken at the narrowest step inside it. Extreme means three or fewer, or one firm holding more than half the stage. High means four to six, with the top two taking most of the revenue. Moderate means seven or more, none of them dominant. Low means many, with the scarce input something another industry sells at volume. Where a figure exists for the top country's share of the segment, it is a second check. When the two disagree, the supplier count wins.
why: The fewer the firms that can do a stage, the more one accident or one license decision affects the whole chain.

aka: Country Group, Country Group D:5, D:5, A:5, D:1, D:3, D:4, arms-embargoed countries
plain: The groups that US export rules sort the world's countries into, published as supplement no. 1 to 15 CFR part 740. A:5 and A:6 list close partners. D:1, D:4 and D:5 are the national security, missile technology and arms-embargoed groups. E:1 and E:2 are the most restricted. A country can be in several groups at once, and the license requirement usually depends on which.
why: US license rules for AI chips are written in terms of these groups. Chips in the 3A090.b band, the band below the top one, need a license for D:1, D:4 and D:5 destinations not also in A:5 or A:6 (15 CFR 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(B)). The UAE moved from D:3 and D:4 into A:5 in July 2026. But the rule names the UAE, so these chips still need a license there, except for approved Emirati consignees (15 CFR 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(B)).

aka: chip on wafer on substrate
plain: TSMC's method for mounting logic chips and memory stacks side by side on a shared interposer, a layer of fine wiring, then mounting that interposer on a rigid base board. In CoWoS-S the interposer is one piece of silicon. In CoWoS-L, used for Nvidia's Blackwell and Rubin, it is layers of fine copper wiring with small embedded silicon bridges. Nearly every high-end AI accelerator is built this way.
why: Epoch AI found that TSMC's CoWoS packaging and memory were the main limits on AI chip production in 2025. It estimates that Nvidia used 60.3 percent of all CoWoS that year. SemiAnalysis judged in March 2026 that CoWoS supply was easing, but in July 2026 TSMC said its packaging capacity was so tight that it limited customers' growth.

aka: Center for Strategic and International Studies
plain: CSIS, the Center for Strategic and International Studies, is a bipartisan, nonprofit policy research organization in Washington, D.C., founded in 1962. Its technology researchers publish assessments of China's chipmaking and of US export controls.
why: Its reports judge how far Chinese chipmakers are from replacing foreign tools. In September 2025 CSIS judged that extreme ultraviolet machines remained firmly out of China's reach despite massive state investment, including $43 billion that China announced for developing its own.

plain: The share of controlled American content a foreign-made item may contain before US export rules, the EAR, apply to it. Under 15 CFR 734.4 the general threshold is 25 percent of the item's value, and 10 percent for the most restricted destinations. Above the threshold the item falls under the EAR, and below it the item does not.
why: It decides whether foreign-made goods with some US content fall under American rules. The foreign direct product rules work differently and catch an item whatever its share of US content. Under 15 CFR 734.4(a)(3), equipment in ECCN 3B993.f.1 has no de minimis level when it is bound for advanced-node chip production. The exception is equipment first exported from a country that also controls it.

aka: D0, defects per square centimeter
plain: The average number of chip-killing flaws per square centimeter of processed wafer. It is a fab's quality score, inferred from how many chips come out working.
why: AI accelerators have some of the largest dies in production, and yield, the share of dies that work, falls steeply as die area times defect density grows. In a textbook example at 0.8 defects per square centimeter, 49.2 percent of dies 1 centimeter on a side come out flawless, against 11.3 percent of dies 2 centimeters on a side. The share that can be sold is higher on chips that carry spare blocks.

plain: An order from BIS that shuts a named party out of trade in US-controlled items, as a sanction or a protective measure, with no license policy involved. Under 15 CFR 764.3 it restricts the party's exports, reexports and in-country transfers of items subject to the EAR, and its access to them. It can also suspend or revoke the party's outstanding licenses. There is no application to file. Orders can be issued outright or suspended and later activated.
why: It can cut a named party off from every item subject to the EAR. The order activated against ZTE in April 2018 stayed in force until BIS terminated it 89 days later as part of a settlement (83 FR 17644; 83 FR 34825).

plain: Adding a layer of material to a wafer. Machines knock atoms off a solid target so they land on the surface, react gases at the surface so a film grows there, or plate metal out of a liquid. It is how the insulators, the wires and the parts of each transistor are built up.
why: Making one chip takes 1,000 to 1,500 steps by a 2025 industry estimate, and many of them are deposition and etch. AI hardware needs films that reach the bottom of deeper holes. Four firms make most of the tools, but deposition is among the tool types where Chinese makers gained the most share between 2019 and 2024.

aka: singular of dice, dies
plain: One rectangular chip cut out of a wafer. Hundreds are printed side by side on the same disc and then sliced apart, and each separated rectangle is a die.
why: Cost and yield are counted per die. A GPU die that fills the largest area one exposure can print loses far more silicon to one fatal defect than a small chip does.

aka: dynamic random-access memory
plain: A computer's main working memory. Each bit is a charge held in a microscopic capacitor that leaks, so the chip has to refresh its contents constantly. It forgets everything when the power goes off.
why: HBM is a stack of DRAM chips, and the three leading DRAM makers, SK hynix, Samsung and Micron, make nearly all of it. SK hynix says the shift of production capacity to HBM left ordinary DRAM, the kind in PCs and phones, undersupplied. The company says the shortage helped drive a significant price recovery from the third quarter of 2025.

aka: deep ultraviolet, deep-ultraviolet, DUV scanner, DUV scanners, DUV tools
plain: Chipmaking light from gas lasers, at 248 or 193 nanometers, and the machines that print with it, which still make up most lithography tools. Filling the gap between lens and wafer with water sharpens the image, a method called immersion.
why: A fab without extreme ultraviolet machines can reach leading-edge logic only with immersion deep ultraviolet and several passes per layer, as SMIC does. So Dutch export licensing covers the most advanced immersion tools.

aka: Export Administration Regulations
plain: The body of US rules that governs the export of commercial goods, software and technology, including items with both civilian and military uses. The Bureau of Industry and Security writes and enforces them. They run from 15 CFR part 730 to part 774. Part 734 sets what they cover, part 742 the license requirements, part 744 the end-use and end-user controls, part 740 the exceptions and part 764 the penalties.
why: American export rules on chips and chipmaking tools are amendments to these regulations, made by notice in the Federal Register with no act of Congress.

plain: The label for an item that falls under US export rules but is not named on the Commerce Control List, the catalog of controlled items. The label is defined at 15 CFR 734.3(c). It is a catch-all category, but an EAR99 item still needs a license if it is going to a listed party or a controlled end use.
why: An EAR99 item can usually ship without a license, but a listed buyer, a controlled end use or an embargoed destination can still require one. So exporters of unlisted items have to follow the end-user controls in part 744 of the EAR too.

aka: Export Control Classification Number
plain: The catalog number that US export rules assign to a controlled item, similar to a customs tariff code but for security-sensitive technology. Number 3A090 covers advanced computing chips and 3B001 covers chipmaking equipment.
why: An item's classification number determines whether it needs a license. So the technical thresholds written into each number set which products are controlled.

aka: electronic design automation, chip design software
plain: The software that turns a description of what a chip should do into the exact pattern of shapes to be printed on silicon. It also proves the design will work before anyone commits money to masks and wafers.
why: Three vendors sell the only software that covers every step of designing a leading-edge chip. Since October 2022 software made for designing chips with gate-all-around transistors has needed a US export license. In May 2025 the US government sent letters to the three vendors requiring a license for all their sales to China, and it lifted the requirement on 2 July.

plain: EMEA stands for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, one region in the breakdowns that companies publish of where their sales go.
why: ASML is based in the Netherlands, yet tools shipped to EMEA made up 1 percent of its net system sales in 2025, against 33 percent for China.

aka: end user, end users, end-user, end use, military end user
plain: Export rules that depend on who the buyer is and what they will do with the item, whatever the item is. The same tool can ship freely to one customer and need a license that will be refused for another.
why: A company can lose access to US-controlled items because of who owns it or what its site produces. In September 2025 US rules were extended to firms at least 50 percent owned by listed entities, though the extension is suspended until 9 November 2026.

aka: entity-list, Entity-Listed, Entity List additions, listed entity, listed entities, listed firm, listed firms
plain: A published list of foreign companies, institutes and individuals. Anyone anywhere, American or foreign, needs a license to send them an item subject to the EAR. Each entry states its own license review policy. Most carry a presumption of denial, meaning the license will normally be refused. SMIC's entry, as amended in December 2024, is a presumption of denial for all items. The exception is tools designed for 200 mm wafer production and bound for a 200 mm plant, which are reviewed case by case. The list is supplement no. 4 to 15 CFR part 744, and the license requirement is in 15 CFR 744.11.
why: It names an organization, so it is one of the simplest tools the US government has. In September 2025 the US extended each listing to companies at least 50 percent owned by listed firms, but that extension is suspended until 9 November 2026 (90 FR 50857).

aka: etching, etched, etches, etcher, etchers, dry etch
plain: Removing material from a wafer wherever the printed pattern says it should not be. Most etch tools turn a gas into a plasma whose ions and fragments eat one material and leave the material beside it alone.
why: Wrap-around transistors need etch that cuts sideways while sparing the material beside it. Stacked memory needs holes far deeper than they are wide. So US rules control etch tools by selectivity, meaning how well a tool cuts one material while sparing another, and by hole shape.

aka: extreme ultraviolet, extreme-ultraviolet, EUV scanner, EUV scanners, extreme ultraviolet lithography
plain: The light that prints the finest layers of every leading-edge chip, and the machines that print with it. Its wavelength is 13.5 nanometers, and shorter light draws finer lines. Air and glass both absorb it, so the machine works in a vacuum and carries the light on mirrors. The light comes from droplets of molten tin, 50,000 a second, each hit twice by a laser.
why: The finest layers set how densely transistors and wires pack, so the most advanced AI chips depend on EUV. Only ASML makes the machines, and export controls block it from shipping them to Chinese chipmakers.

aka: fabrication plant, wafer fab, fabs, chip factory, chip factories
plain: The factory where wafers are processed into chips. It is a cleanroom where each wafer moves from machine to machine in a sealed pod for months. The building costs tens of billions of dollars.
why: In 2023 BCG estimated that a new 2 nm-class fab finished in 2026 would cost $35 to $43 billion to own over ten years. SemiAnalysis judged in December 2025 that finding enough workers remained a major challenge for TSMC in Arizona. TSMC has yet to build one of its largest fabs outside Taiwan.

plain: A chip company that designs and sells chips but owns no factory, paying a contract manufacturer, a foundry, to make them. Nvidia, AMD, Apple, Qualcomm and Broadcom all work this way.
why: The fabless model concentrates manufacturing in a handful of foundries. So a designer's supply, its costs and where its chips are made all depend on a company it does not control.

aka: fin field-effect transistor
plain: A transistor whose channel, the strip that current flows through, stands on edge like a shark fin. The gate, the electrode that switches the current, wraps around three sides of the fin instead of resting on one. More contact means firmer control and less leakage when the switch is meant to be off.
why: TSMC's leading-edge processes used FinFETs until N2, its first process with gate-all-around transistors, entered volume production in late 2025. The October 2022 US rules used FinFET or 16/14 nm logic as one of their thresholds for an advanced fab.

aka: floating point operations per second, TFLOPS, PFLOPS, FLOP, teraflops
plain: A count of how many arithmetic operations on floating-point numbers, numbers with a fractional part, a chip can perform each second, the way horsepower counts an engine's output.
why: It is the standard unit of AI compute, but two chips' figures can be compared only when the number format behind each, such as 8-bit or 16-bit, is stated. US export rules use their own score, TPP, which weights each operation by its bit length.

aka: FDPR, FDP rule, foreign-produced direct product rule, direct product rule, foreign-produced item rules, foreign-produced item rule, foreign-produced item
plain: A US rule that puts a foreign-made item under American control when two tests are both met. The first is about the product: the item was made directly from specified US technology or software, or in a plant that was. The second is about the destination: the item is going somewhere, or to someone, the rule names. The mechanics are in 15 CFR 734.9.
why: The rule lets US controls reach goods made outside the United States. Without it, a buyer on the Entity List could escape US controls by ordering chips from a supplier outside the United States. With it, a chip made in Taiwan on American tools for Huawei needs a US license. For listed firms the rule reaches only those whose entry carries a footnote naming it, such as Huawei's (15 CFR 734.9(e)).

aka: pure-play foundry, contract chipmaker, foundries, pure-play, pure play, pure-play model, contract chipmaking
plain: A company, or a division of one, that manufactures chips designed by other companies. A pure-play foundry, the model TSMC pioneered after its founding in 1987, makes no products of its own. The model works because no chip company sells enough of one product to fill a modern fab on its own.
why: All six of TSMC's largest plants are in Taiwan. Taiwan held 69 percent of the world's logic capacity below 10 nm in 2022, so political events there affect the whole chip supply.

aka: 8-bit and 4-bit floating point, FP8, FP4, FP16, BF16, INT8, number formats
plain: Ways of writing a number using only 8 or 4 binary digits, or bits, far fewer than standard formats use. Each number is less precise, but the chip can perform and store far more of them. That trade-off suits machine learning, which can work with less exact numbers.
why: Lower precision raises a chip's headline speed, so a performance figure quoted without its number format cannot be compared. US export rules allow for this by weighting each operation by its bit length.

aka: GAA, nanosheet transistor, RibbonFET at Intel, nanosheet, nanosheets, RibbonFET, GAA transistor, gate-all-around transistors
plain: A transistor in which the gate, the electrode that switches the current, wraps all the way around the channel that current flows through. In a FinFET, the design it replaces, the gate touches three sides. Surrounding the channel gives the gate firmer control than a fin allows, so less current leaks when the switch is off.
why: Only TSMC, Intel and Samsung make it in volume. It needs etch that cuts sideways, which US export rules control. Customers building 2 nm gate-all-around capacity lifted ASM International, the leader in atomic layer deposition, to record revenue in 2025.

aka: graphics processing unit, GPUs
plain: A processor originally built to draw video game images by doing thousands of simple calculations at once. Neural networks turned out to need the same kind of arithmetic, so the GPU became the default AI processor.
why: Nvidia used 60.3 percent of all CoWoS packaging in 2025, on Epoch AI's estimate. The US required a license for Nvidia's H20 in April 2025. Since January 2026 it has reviewed applications to sell the H200 to buyers in China case by case.

plain: The share of a sale left over after paying what it cost to make the thing, before research, sales and overheads are counted. A 70 percent gross margin means $70 of every $100 of revenue is left after manufacturing cost.
why: Gross margin shows which firms have pricing power. In quarters ending June to September 2026, Micron's was 86.8 percent and Nvidia's 75.0 percent. The assembly and test houses Amkor and ASE were at 16.8 to 27.3 percent, counting ASE's packaging and test segment alone.

aka: high bandwidth memory, high-bandwidth memory, HBM3E, HBM4, HBM4E, HBM stack, HBM stacks, memory stacks, stacked memory
plain: Stacked memory built for AI chips. Up to sixteen memory chips are stacked into a cube and wired together through copper-filled holes made in each chip before stacking. The cube sits a few millimeters from the processor. It holds the model the chip is running, the numbers called weights, and hands them to the processor over 1,024 or more wires at once.
why: To write each word of an answer, the chip reads the whole model from this memory, along with the record of the conversation so far. A larger model or a longer conversation needs more memory, so the size and speed of HBM usually set how many people one chip can serve. HBM is the largest line in the bill of materials of an Nvidia B200. SK hynix, Samsung and Micron make nearly all of it.

aka: high numerical aperture extreme ultraviolet, ASML EXE series, High-NA, High NA, High-NA scanners, High-NA machine, High-NA tools
plain: The next generation of extreme ultraviolet machine, whose larger mirrors collect light over a wider angle and so print smaller features. The wider optics also halve the area the machine can print in one exposure, so a large chip has to be stitched together from two exposures.
why: It cuts the smallest printable feature from 13 nanometers to 8, and TSMC expects more AI chip layers to need it. Each machine sells for an estimated $350 to $400 million. Intel says it uses High-NA in volume production for select layers of some 18A products. TSMC plans to use it in high-volume manufacturing from 2030.

aka: direct bond interconnect, SoIC, Foveros Direct, copper pad to copper pad
plain: Joining two chips by bonding their copper pads, and the glass-like insulator around them, directly to each other, with no solder in between. Removing the solder lets connections be packed much more tightly and shortens the path heat has to travel out.
why: An SK hynix tech note puts microbumps about 20 micrometers apart and hybrid-bonded pads under 1 micrometer apart. It expects full-scale use in HBM at HBM4E or HBM5, where stacks are projected to pass twenty layers.

aka: hyperscalers
plain: One of the handful of companies that run data centers at global scale, such as Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta and Oracle.
why: They pay for the AI buildout. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle spent $448.2 billion of capital in 2025, the sum of Epoch AI's quarterly figures.

aka: integrated device manufacturer, integrated device maker, integrated device makers
plain: A chip company that both designs its products and manufactures them in its own factories. Intel, Samsung and Micron are examples.
why: An integrated maker that also makes chips for other companies competes with its own customers. Its own products take the best capacity, so fewer customers trust it with a flagship design.

aka: transfer (in-country)
plain: A change in the end use or the end user of an item inside one foreign country, defined at 15 CFR 734.16. Nothing crosses a border. A server legally imported into a country for one customer is transferred when it is resold, or repurposed, for another.
why: Controls on in-country transfers catch hardware diverted after it has arrived. So a license granted for a named Chinese customer does not cover the hardware if it passes to someone else. Reexports and in-country transfers of advanced chips to Macau or Country Group D:5 keep a presumption of denial, meaning a license will normally be refused (91 FR 1684). That holds even where an export from the United States would be reviewed case by case (91 FR 1684).

aka: interposers, silicon interposer, silicon carrier
plain: A layer of wiring with no transistors, used as a miniature circuit board underneath several chips so they can be connected at a density no ordinary board could reach. It is either one piece of silicon or layers of fine copper wiring, often with small silicon bridges.
why: HBM connects over 1,024 or 2,048 wires, too many for a resin board, so memory and logic sit together on an interposer. Its area caps how much fits in one package. In April 2026 TSMC was producing CoWoS at 5.5 times the reticle, the largest area a lithography machine prints in one exposure.

aka: is informed letter, is-informed letters, by letter
plain: A letter from BIS to one named company imposing a license requirement on a specific export, without any rule being published. BIS's power to send one is written into the regulations themselves, for example 15 CFR 744.23(b), which lets BIS inform a person individually, with no amendment to the EAR.
why: It imposes a control at once, with no published rule. BIS imposed the April 2025 license requirement for Nvidia's H20 this way, and the public learned of it from Nvidia's own filing.

aka: KGD, good die, good dies, known good die
plain: A bare chip tested thoroughly enough, before assembly, to be trusted inside something expensive. In an ordinary product a faulty chip wastes one chip. Inside a package that joins a dozen expensive pieces, one bad die throws away all of them.
why: As packages grow toward about ten large compute dies and 20 memory stacks, a bad die found only after assembly scraps more parts. So chipmakers move testing and burn-in, running chips hot to force early failures, back onto the wafer.

aka: license exception
plain: A written carve-out in export rules that lets a shipment go without an individual license, if it meets stated conditions. The ones that matter for AI chips and chipmaking tools are NAC and ACA (15 CFR 740.8), HBM (740.25), AIA and LPP (740.27 and 740.29), IEC (740.24) and RPL (740.10). AIA and LPP let the top band of accelerators ship to allies, and elsewhere in small volumes. IEC covers countries that adopt matching controls, and RPL covers servicing and spare parts.
why: Exceptions let the US government adjust its controls without rewriting them and ease the rules for allies. License Exception IEC, added in September 2024, covers exports to and by countries that have put equivalent controls in place (89 FR 72926).

aka: ACA, Advanced Computing Authorized
plain: An export rule that lets AI chips other than top-band data center chips ship to most of the world with no license and no advance notice. It covers the same chips as its companion exception NAC, and every destination except Macau, Country Group D:5 and firms headquartered in either. The top-band data center chips in ECCN 3A090.a are excluded. BIS split it from NAC at 15 CFR 740.8 in April 2024. The AI Diffusion rule widened it in January 2025 to the whole world outside Macau and D:5.
why: It lets these chips reach most of the world with no license or advance notice. NAC keeps a notice requirement for Macau and D:5. Before April 2024 NAC did both jobs, so an older table that shows one exception describes what is now two.

plain: An export rule that lets high bandwidth memory go to a packaging site with no license, to be packaged beside a chip. It applies if the memory's bandwidth density is below 3.3 GB/s per square millimeter, measured over the area of the package or stack. The exporter must be headquartered in the United States or Country Group A:5. If the memory is bound for Macau or Country Group D:5, the chip's designer must buy it. The stacks must go straight to the packaging site. It does not cover packaging at a facility in Macau or D:5 that also makes advanced-node chips. It sits at 15 CFR 740.25.
why: It lets Chinese packaging houses stay in the supply chain of American and allied chip designers. But a sale of the same stacks to a Chinese buyer still needs a license. HBM needs a license only for Macau and Country Group D:5, and the exception was written into the December 2024 rule that first controlled HBM (89 FR 96790).

aka: LPP, Low Processing Performance
plain: An export rule that lets a buyer almost anywhere receive a capped amount of top-band AI chips each year without a license. The cap is 26,900,000 TPP, the export rules' measure of computing power, per ultimate consignee per calendar year. Macau, Country Group D:5 and firms headquartered in either are excluded, and it does not cover transfers within a country. The AI Diffusion rule created it in January 2025, at 15 CFR 740.29.
why: It lets buyers outside the nineteen destinations in supplement no. 5 to part 740 take top AI chips in small amounts with no license application. BIS said in May 2025 that it would not enforce the AI Diffusion rule, but it withdrew none of the text. So LPP still stands in the regulations beside the rule's other exceptions, AIA and ACM, and the nineteen-destination list.

aka: NAC, Notified Advanced Computing
plain: An export rule that lets AI chips other than top-band data center chips ship to Macau and Country Group D:5, and to firms headquartered there, with no license. The exporter must notify BIS at least 25 calendar days ahead, and the shipment can go if BIS does not say a license is needed. The top-band data center chips in ECCN 3A090.a and the memory in 3A090.c are excluded. It sits at 15 CFR 740.8.
why: It lets these chips reach the restricted destinations without a license application. Since April 2024 section 740.8 has held two exceptions, NAC for the restricted destinations and ACA for everywhere else.

aka: direct-to-chip cooling, cold plate cooling, cold plate, cold plates, liquid-cooled, direct-to-chip liquid, direct liquid cooling
plain: Taking heat out of a processor by pumping liquid through a cold plate on the chip package, instead of blowing air across a finned heatsink. A building loop then carries the heat outdoors.
why: Nvidia's GB300 NVL72 rack is liquid cooled, and its Rubin platform is entirely liquid cooled. Nvidia says every cloud provider and data center operator building for Rubin is moving to liquid cooling.

aka: photolithography
plain: Printing a circuit pattern onto a wafer by shining light through a patterned plate and projecting a shrunken image of it onto a light-sensitive coating. It works like photography at the scale of nanometers, repeated once for every layer of the chip.
why: Only one company, ASML, makes the machines for its finest layers, and those layers set how densely transistors and wires pack.

aka: logic chips, logic die, logic dies
plain: A logic chip is one that computes, such as a processor, a graphics processor or an AI accelerator. Memory chips, such as DRAM and NAND flash, store data instead.
why: US export rules set separate lines for logic and memory. The October 2022 rule covered equipment for fabs in China making logic chips at 16/14 nm or below. It also covered fabs making DRAM at 18 nm half-pitch or below, or NAND with 128 or more layers. ASML's 2025 system sales were €16,054.1 million to logic chipmakers and €8,420.2 million to memory makers.

plain: The widening gap between how fast a processor can calculate and how fast memory can feed it numbers to work on. The cost of arithmetic has fallen faster than the cost of moving numbers.
why: An AI chip reads its whole model from memory for each word it writes, so memory size and speed usually set how many people one chip can serve. Memory is also about half the cost of building an Nvidia B200, on Epoch AI's estimate.

aka: process control, when grouped with inspection, metrology and inspection, inspection tools
plain: Measuring what a factory actually built: how wide a printed line came out, how thick a film is, whether this layer sits exactly on top of the last one. Inspection is the related job of finding flaws.
why: A fab that cannot buy sensitive inspection tools finds fewer of the defects that lower its yield, so its yield rises more slowly. KLA held 56.8 percent of the market for these tools in 2025, by CSET's count.

aka: double patterning, quadruple patterning, self-aligned double patterning, self-aligned quadruple patterning, SADP, SAQP, LELE, multiple patterning, multi-patterning, several passes, several exposures, multiply exposed, DUV multipatterning
plain: Building one chip layer in several patterning steps, because a single exposure cannot print lines that close together. It comes in two kinds. Litho-etch multipatterning splits the layer's pattern across two or three masks, then prints and etches each part separately. Self-aligned double or quadruple patterning prints one coarser pattern, then deposits and etches thin spacer films along its edges to halve or quarter the line spacing. Cut masks then remove the parts of lines the circuit does not need.
why: SMIC makes its 7 nm-class chips without extreme ultraviolet machines by multipatterning on deep ultraviolet tools. TSMC's first 7 nm process and Intel 7 were also made without extreme ultraviolet light. Every extra mask or spacer step adds cost and machine time, and each extra litho-etch exposure adds a chance that parts of the layer misalign.

aka: process node, technology node, for example N2 or 18A, nodes
plain: The name a foundry gives one generation of its manufacturing process. The number in the name no longer measures anything on the chip. SMIC's N+3, a 7 nm-class process, spaces its narrowest wires closer together than Intel's Panther Lake chips on 18A do.
why: Comparing two foundries by node name says little. Each foundry also picks its own baseline for the density gains it claims.

aka: GB200 NVL72, GB300 NVL72, Vera Rubin NVL72
plain: Nvidia's rack-sized product, with 72 accelerators in 18 compute trays joined through nine switch trays so that software can treat the whole rack as one computer. The GB300 version draws up to 142 kilowatts.
why: AI capacity is built and costed by the rack. In July 2026 SemiAnalysis put the cost of owning a Vera Rubin NVL72 at $3.57 per GPU-hour, against $1.84 for a GB200 and $2.36 for a GB300.

aka: NVSwitch, NVLink 5, NVLink 6, NV-HBI
plain: Nvidia's own high-speed connection between its accelerators, which lets dozens of them act as one. NVLink 6 carries 3,600 gigabytes per second per GPU, according to Nvidia's January 2026 Rubin launch.
why: Nvidia controls it, while more than 50 makers of systems and components build around its racks. Since May 2025 its NVLink Fusion program has let other firms' custom chips connect to Nvidia GPUs over NVLink, and Fujitsu and Qualcomm plan CPUs that do so. UALink is a published open rival.

aka: optical module, pluggable optics, optical transceivers, transceiver, transceivers, optical modules, 800G optical transceivers
plain: A small device that turns electrical signals into laser light for sending down a glass fiber, and turns them back at the far end. Every network link longer than a few meters in a large AI cluster needs one at each end.
why: A cluster needs several for each accelerator. One design for 100,000 H100s uses 98,304 just to link its GPUs to the first tier of switches. Chinese firms assemble the modules in volume, but the lasers inside them were scarce in 2026.

aka: outsourced semiconductor assembly and test, OSATs, outsourced assembly and test, assembly and test firms, assembly and test contractor, assembly and test houses
plain: A contract firm that takes finished wafers, cuts them into chips, seals the chips into packages and tests them. It is the back end of chipmaking, done for hire.
why: Every chip passes through assembly and test. Yet in the June 2026 quarter Amkor earned a gross margin of 16.8 percent, and ASE's packaging and test segment 27.3 percent. In a TrendForce ranking cited by CSET, four of the ten largest of these firms by 2024 revenue are headquartered in China.

aka: overlay error, alignment
plain: How precisely one printed layer of a chip lands on top of the layer beneath it. Before each exposure the scanner finds marks printed in earlier layers and lines the new layer up on them to within a few nanometers, across a disc 300 millimeters wide.
why: Misalignment can ruin whole regions of a wafer, so overlay is one of the specifications that separates an advanced printing machine from an ordinary one. Each extra pass on a layer is another chance to misalign.

aka: pellicles, EUV pellicle
plain: A thin transparent membrane on a frame above a photomask, the patterned plate a chip layer is printed from. Dust settles on it, far enough out of focus that it does not print, so the pattern stays clean. It works like a lens cap a photographer can shoot through.
why: Pellicles already work in high-volume EUV manufacturing. But no material is completely transparent to EUV light, and the light crosses the membrane twice, so every pellicle costs some output. Carbon nanotube membranes, which passed up to 97 percent of the light in one crossing in imec's 2020 tests, are the next step.

plain: An export control test of how densely a chip packs its computing power. It divides the chip's TPP, the export rules' measure of computing power, by its applicable die area in square millimeters. That area counts all logic dies made on a process with non-planar transistors, such as FinFETs. The test applies only to a chip that reaches 1,600 TPP. It replaced the 2022 test, which was based on interconnect bandwidth, the speed at which a chip exchanges data with its neighbors.
why: It closed a gap that Nvidia's China-specific chips, such as the A800 and H800, had used. Nvidia had designed those chips to stay under the 2022 interconnect-speed threshold. The top band, ECCN 3A090.a, now starts at 4,800 TPP, or at 1,600 TPP with a performance density of 5.92 (88 FR 73458).

aka: mask, reticle, mask set, photomasks, masks, mask sets, mask blank set
plain: The master template for one layer of a chip: a quartz plate, or for the shortest wavelengths a mirror, that carries the pattern projected onto the wafer. A chip needs dozens of them, at least one per layer. In July 2022 SemiAnalysis put a full set above $1 million at 28 nm and above $10 million at 7 nm. In May 2026 it put a leading-edge set at $40 million.
why: The cost of a mask set limits which chips are worth making on a leading-edge process at all. Only three firms supply the blank plates for EUV masks, and two of them are Japanese.

aka: resist, resists, EUV resist, EUV resists, resist makers
plain: The light-sensitive coating that records a chip's pattern during lithography. A machine spins a thin film of it across the wafer. Light shone through a stencil changes the film where it lands, and a wash removes those parts. What remains shows the next machine where to etch.
why: Every printed layer of a chip uses it. Each resist is tuned to the layers it prints, and even one that passes the first time takes seven to 17 months to approve in a fab. Japanese companies held 78 percent of world sales in 2023. In 2024 an investment vehicle of a Japanese state-backed fund bought 84.36 percent of the resist maker JSR.

plain: A license review policy in which the reviewing agencies start from the position that an application should be refused. An application can still be filed and will be considered, but the exporter has to overcome that starting position. It is the general policy for advanced computing chips going to China and Macau under 15 CFR 742.6(b)(10), and for most Entity List entries. Since January 2026 export applications for some less powerful chips, such as the H200, are reviewed case by case instead.
why: The difference between a presumption of denial and a prohibition decides whether a company files at all. Under a presumption of denial an application can still be made, but under a prohibition it cannot.

aka: probe cards
plain: A circuit board carrying thousands of fine needles that press onto the contact pads of a chip while it is still part of the wafer. A tester drives signals into the chip through the needles. Every card is custom-built for one chip design.
why: Because each card is custom-built and slow to qualify, probe card supply and lead time can limit how fast a new accelerator or memory stack reaches full production.

aka: cabinet, racks, cabinets, rack-scale
plain: The standard steel frame that computing equipment is bolted into in a data center, roughly the size of a wardrobe. For AI, a whole rack is wired and sold as one machine, so the rack itself is the product.
why: A GB300 NVL72 rack draws up to 142 kilowatts. Nvidia's 800-volt power design is intended for racks of more than a megawatt from 2027. A megawatt rack needs a different busbar, the metal bar that carries power to its equipment. It also changes the weight the floor must bear, the coolant flow and the energy stored in the rack to keep its power draw steady.

plain: Shipping an item that falls under US export rules, the EAR, from one foreign country to another. The term is defined at 15 CFR 734.14. A memory stack subject to the EAR moving from Korea to China is a reexport, and it needs the same US license a shipment from Texas would.
why: The reexport rule lets US controls follow an item after it leaves the United States, so they reach trade between two foreign countries.

aka: photomask
plain: The patterned plate whose image a lithography machine projects onto the wafer, one chip layer at a time. In practice it means the same as photomask, but the word reticle stresses that the machine steps the same image again and again across the wafer.
why: One exposure from a reticle prints at most 26 by 33 millimeters of the wafer, and every large AI chip has to be designed around that limit.

aka: reticle size limit, reticle field, field size, reticle-limited, reticle size, reticles, times reticle
plain: The largest chip a lithography machine can print in a single exposure, about 858 square millimeters, or 26 by 33 millimeters. It is set by the machine's optics and is the same for every design. The newer High-NA EUV machines print half that area.
why: Many leading AI accelerators, Nvidia's Blackwell among them, need more circuitry than this, so they are split into several dies, separate pieces of silicon, and joined back together inside a package.

aka: back-end network, cluster fabric, scale-out, scale out
plain: The network that joins thousands of accelerator groups into one cluster, running at hundreds of gigabits per second over Ethernet or InfiniBand. Its Ethernet versions use the same standard as ordinary data center networks.
why: It lets thousands of accelerators train one model together. InfiniBand was the main scale-out network when AI clusters were small. But Ethernet capacity has since grown quickly, as Broadcom doubled the bandwidth of its switch chips every generation.

aka: scale-up fabric, coherent domain, scale-up, scale up, scale-up domain, scale-up switch
plain: The network that joins a group of accelerators, from a few dozen in one rack to thousands, so a model too large for a single chip can be spread across them. It runs at terabytes per second. In Nvidia's GB300 NVL72 each GPU has nine times as much bandwidth on it as on the scale-out network.
why: The bandwidth of this network limits how efficiently a large model trains. Nvidia sells its own NVLink for it, and UALink is a published open standard that competes with NVLink.

plain: The argument that Taiwan's lead in advanced chipmaking deters an attack on the island, because so many countries rely on its chips.
why: The idea is central to debate about Taiwan's security, and it is contested. It holds only while Taiwan's chipmaking is hard to replace, so Taiwan keeps its newest chip processes at home first while the United States pushes for more chipmaking on its own soil.

aka: small yard with a high fence, small yard
plain: The stated design of US technology controls: tightly restrict a narrow set of items that genuinely matter to national security, and leave the rest of trade alone.
why: It gives critics and defenders a test for whether export controls remain targeted security policy or have become general industrial policy.

aka: system on a chip, system-on-chip, system-on-a-chip, SoCs
plain: A system on a chip, or SoC, is a single chip that combines processor cores, a graphics processor and other circuit blocks that a device needs. The main processor in a smartphone is one.
why: Makers of chip testers split their market in two. SoC testers check processors and other non-memory chips, and memory testers check memory. Advantest put SoC testers at about $6.9 billion of a $9.0 billion tester market in 2025.

plain: The test for whether an item falls under US export rules at all. Under 15 CFR 734.3 it covers anything in the United States and anything of US origin wherever it is. It also covers foreign-made goods that contain more than a permitted share of controlled US content, and foreign-made goods caught by a foreign direct product rule. The test applies to the item, whatever the seller's nationality.
why: The rules follow the item, so a Dutch or Korean firm shipping between two foreign countries can still need a US license.

aka: substitutability rating
plain: A four-band rating of how hard it would be for a well-funded state or firm, starting today, to build an alternative to the leading suppliers at one stage of the supply chain. It is judged against four written tests. Easy: a second supplier is qualified, meaning approved by customers, and shipping today at the leading node, the most advanced process. Moderate: a second supplier exists but is not yet qualified at the leading node, and closing the gap takes about two to five years. Hard: no second supplier exists at the leading node, the path to one is known, and closing the gap takes five to ten years. Very hard: no second supplier exists, and the path depends on physics, decades of unwritten know-how or protected intellectual property. No one has yet repeated what the leaders did, and closing the gap takes ten years or more. The years are always counted for that same well-funded state or firm, and the count stops at qualification, which comes well after a prototype.
why: It says how long a rival or a government would need to replace a stage. The debate over export controls turns on that question.

aka: package substrate, IC substrate, substrates, build-up substrate, build-up substrates, package substrates, IC substrates, resin substrate
plain: The small, dense circuit board at the base of a chip package. The chips sit on it, and it spreads their microscopic connections out to the millimeter-scale solder balls a motherboard can accept. It is built up layer by layer from epoxy film, laser-drilled holes and plated copper.
why: A handful of firms, most of them in Asia, build these substrates for others. As packages grow, a substrate warps more and needs more layers, so fewer come out working.

aka: tape out, taped out, tapes out, tape-outs, tapeout
plain: The moment a chip design is declared finished and the pattern files are sent to the factory to be written into masks. The name survives from when the data physically left on a reel of magnetic tape.
why: Each revision after tape-out, called a respin, needs at least some new masks. In May 2026 SemiAnalysis put a single respin at leading-edge nodes at $50 million to $100 million, so designers check everything they can before tape-out.

aka: total processing performance
plain: Total processing performance, the measure US export rules use for a chip's computing power. It starts from the number of multiply-accumulate operations, a multiply followed by an add, that the chip does each second. That number is doubled, multiplied by the number of bits in each operation, and added up across every processing unit on the chip. The definition is in ECCN 3A090, in supplement no. 1 to 15 CFR part 774.
why: The export rules for chip sales to China draw their lines in TPP. The top band, 3A090.a, starts at 4,800 TPP, or at 1,600 TPP with a performance density of 5.92. Since 15 January 2026, export applications for chips below 21,000 TPP and 6,500 GB/s of total DRAM bandwidth, such as the H200, are reviewed case by case for end users in China and Macau (91 FR 1684).

aka: Tensor Processing Unit, TPUs
plain: Google's own AI chip, designed in-house for its data centers and cloud service. Its eighth generation, announced in April 2026, is split into two chips, the TPU 8t for training and the TPU 8i for inference.
why: It shows that a large buyer can design its own alternative to chips sold on the open market. Ironwood, the seventh generation, carries 192 GB of memory per chip, six times its predecessor's. Google says the TPU 8t and TPU 8i deliver up to twice Ironwood's performance per watt.

aka: transistors
plain: The switch every chip is built from. Current runs through a channel between two terminals. A voltage on a third terminal, the gate, opens or closes that path, much as a tap opens or closes a pipe. One Nvidia Blackwell part contains 208 billion of them.
why: The whole chip supply chain exists to make transistors smaller, faster and less leaky. Only three companies, TSMC, Intel and Samsung, make the newest kind in volume.

aka: through-silicon via, TSVs, through-silicon vias, through silicon via, through silicon vias
plain: A copper column that runs all the way through a chip so that power and signals can pass from its top face to its bottom face. It makes stacking chips vertically possible, in the way an elevator shaft makes a tall building usable.
why: High bandwidth memory depends on these columns. US rules control the tools that cut the holes for them, and define those tools by hole shape and etching speed.

aka: Validated End-User, Validated End User, Validated End-User status, VEU status, VEU cover, validated end users
plain: An authorization that BIS, the US Commerce Department office that licenses exports, grants to a named foreign facility, so approved items can ship to it without an individual license each time. The approved facilities are listed in supplement no. 7 to 15 CFR part 748, and the procedure is set out in 15 CFR 748.15.
why: It let the China subsidiaries of Samsung and SK hynix, and the Dalian NAND flash memory fab that SK hynix bought from Intel, receive US equipment without individual licenses. BIS revoked that status effective 31 December 2025 (90 FR 42321). It said it would license those fabs to keep running, but not to expand capacity or upgrade technology (90 FR 42321). In December 2025 BIS granted SK hynix an annual license to ship approved US equipment to its China fabs during 2026.

aka: silicon wafer, 300 mm wafer, wafers, silicon wafers, 300 mm wafers
plain: The polished disc of ultrapure silicon that chips are built on, 300 millimeters across for advanced chips. Hundreds of chips are printed on one wafer and cut apart at the end.
why: A flaw wastes more silicon on a large AI chip than on a small one, so AI chips need wafers that are nearly flawless and flat to the edge. The top five wafer makers hold around 75 percent of a market worth $11.4 billion in 2025.

aka: WFE, front-end equipment, equipment billings, wafer processing equipment, semiconductor equipment, chipmaking tools, chipmaking equipment
plain: The collective name for the machines that process wafers inside a fab: printing systems, deposition and etch chambers, cleaning tools and measurement systems. It excludes the packaging and test machines used afterward.
why: Spending on it shows how much new chipmaking capacity is being built. World sales of all chipmaking equipment reached $135.1 billion in 2025, and sales of wafer processing tools rose 12 percent.

aka: die yield, yields, packaging yield, package yield, stack yield
plain: The percentage of chips on a wafer that work. Flaws land at random, so the larger the chip the more likely it is to catch one, and yield falls steeply as chips get bigger.
why: Yield sets the cost of a working AI chip. Epoch AI models the Blackwell compute die at 40 to 70 percent good, with 60 percent as its central estimate. In the same model, the cost of packages that fail testing, spread across the ones that pass, adds about $1,000 to each B200.

aka: chemical mechanical polishing, chemical mechanical planarization, polishing slurry, polishing slurries, slurry, slurries, CMP slurry, CMP pads, planarization
plain: Chemical mechanical polishing, or CMP, rubs a wafer's surface flat again after each new layer goes on, using a pad and a liquid full of fine grit called slurry. Without it the next layer would be printed on a surface too bumpy to focus on.
why: Japanese companies held 51 percent of polishing-slurry sales in 2023, counted by company nationality. CSET's January 2021 brief, drawing on 2019 market reports, put DuPont and Cabot Microelectronics at about 56 percent of a $790 million slurry market. Cabot was renamed CMC Materials in October 2020, and Entegris bought it in July 2022. DuPont's electronics business became Qnity Electronics in November 2025.

aka: ion implanter, ion implanters, implant, implant layers, implantation
plain: A way of changing how silicon conducts by firing atoms into it. An ion implanter shoots charged atoms of boron, phosphorus or arsenic into the wafer, where they lodge just under the surface. The patches they land in then conduct the way the design needs.
why: Every modern chip process relies on it. Implanters are export-controlled. In February 2026 Applied Materials agreed to pay a penalty of about $252 million over implanters shipped to a Chinese customer on the Entity List.

aka: epitaxial, epitaxial wafer, epitaxial wafers, epitaxial layer, epi
plain: Epitaxy grows a fresh layer of crystal on top of a wafer, atom by atom, so the new layer continues the crystal beneath it with almost no flaws. An epitaxial wafer is a plain wafer with that extra layer, and the transistors are built in it.
why: Flaws in that layer can make the transistors leak current. The industry association SEMI credits the 2025 rise in wafer shipments to AI demand for advanced epitaxial wafers for logic chips and polished wafers for high-bandwidth memory.

aka: polycrystalline silicon, electronic-grade polysilicon, semiconductor-grade polysilicon, polysilicon feedstock
plain: Polysilicon is purified silicon that has not yet been grown into one crystal. It comes as gray rods made of many small crystals. It is the raw material that is melted down to pull the single crystal a wafer is cut from. The same material, at lower purity, goes into solar panels.
why: China made about 93 percent of the world's polysilicon in 2023. But the German wafer maker Siltronic names five major suppliers of the electronic-grade kind for 2025, and none of them is Chinese.

aka: electronic grade, semiconductor-grade, semiconductor grade, solar-grade, solar grade
plain: Electronic-grade, or semiconductor-grade, silicon is refined until its metal impurities are no more than a few parts per billion, pure enough for chips. Solar-grade silicon is a less pure grade made for solar cells.
why: Every chip starts from it. The Commerce Department found in 2026 that semiconductor-grade polysilicon makes up only 2.4 percent of global production. The German wafer maker Siltronic names five major suppliers for 2025: Wacker, Hemlock, OCI, Tokuyama and Mitsubishi. None of them is Chinese.

aka: immersion DUV, ArF immersion, immersion scanner, immersion scanners, immersion tools, immersion DUV scanners, immersion deep-ultraviolet
plain: Immersion lithography prints with a thin layer of ultrapure water between the scanner's lens and the wafer. The water lets the lens focus light at a wider angle than air allows, so the same light prints finer lines. It is the most advanced form of deep ultraviolet lithography, one step below extreme ultraviolet.
why: Dutch export licensing covers the most advanced immersion scanners. Reuters reported in July 2026, citing one unnamed source, that a Chinese state-owned firm had started producing its own immersion scanners.

aka: argon fluoride, argon fluoride laser, 193 nm, 193-nanometer
plain: ArF stands for argon fluoride, the gas mixture inside the laser that gives deep ultraviolet lithography its 193-nanometer light. Scanners, the machines that print each layer, use this light in two ways. A dry scanner shines it through air, and an immersion scanner through a thin film of water between lens and wafer, which prints finer lines. ArF scanners print most of the fine layers on any chip made without extreme ultraviolet.
why: ArF immersion scanners made up 42 percent of ASML's system sales in 2025. They are also the kind that a Chinese state-owned firm was reported in July 2026 to be producing at home.

aka: krypton fluoride, krypton fluoride laser, 248 nm, 248-nanometer
plain: KrF is krypton fluoride, the gas in an older lithography laser that shines at 248 nanometers. KrF scanners print the coarser layers of a chip, where lines are far apart.
why: KrF tools print coarser layers such as implant layers. ASML sold 78 of them in 2025, and Canon also makes them.

aka: g-line, i-line steppers, i-line scanners
plain: i-line is the coarsest of the main lithography lights, 365 nanometers from a mercury lamp, named for one line in the lamp's spectrum. It prints the widest features on a chip and much of a package.
why: SMEE, the established Chinese scanner maker, is strongest in i-line, and even there it holds about 4 percent of the world market.

aka: scanners, stepper, steppers, lithography scanner, lithography scanners, lithography machine, lithography system, lithography systems
plain: A scanner is the lithography machine itself. It holds the photomask up to a light source and projects a shrunken image of one layer onto the wafer. Mask and wafer sweep past each other in a narrow slit of light. An older stepper exposes the whole mask image at once instead of scanning. A standard EUV scanner sells for around $200 million.
why: ASML makes every EUV scanner in the world, so a rule aimed at its scanners reaches all advanced chipmaking.

aka: plasmas, plasma etch, plasma-enhanced, plasma source
plain: A plasma is a gas energized until some of its atoms or molecules break into charged particles. Most etch steps and many deposition steps happen in a plasma that an electric field makes inside a vacuum chamber, though batch furnaces mostly work without one. In the chamber, neutral fragments called radicals do most of the chemistry, and charged ions give etch its direction. In an extreme ultraviolet machine, a laser vaporizes droplets of molten tin into a plasma that gives off the 13.5-nanometer light.
why: Export controls describe each tool by the process it is designed to run. An extreme ultraviolet source has to make its tin plasma 50,000 times a second to give enough light for production.

aka: electron-beam, e-beam, electron beams, multi-beam, multibeam, e-beam inspection, electron-beam metrology
plain: An electron beam is a stream of electrons focused to a spot far smaller than any spot of light. Mask shops use it to write the pattern onto a photomask, and fabs use it to inspect wafers for defects light cannot see and to measure line widths. A multi-beam tool fires many beams at once, because a single beam is slow.
why: In 2023 Intel called Austria's IMS Nanofabrication the established leader in the multi-beam writers that advanced EUV masks require. Since December 2024 US rules have controlled wafer inspection tools that use two or more beams to find defects 21 nm across or smaller.

aka: mask writers, multi-beam writer, multi-beam writers, electron-beam writer, e-beam writer, mask writing
plain: A mask writer is the machine that uses electrons to draw a chip's pattern into the resist on a photomask blank. A single-beam writer flashes one shape at a time, while NuFlare's multi-beam writer for the most advanced masks controls 260,000 beams at once.
why: No new chip can be printed until its masks are written. In 2023 Intel said advanced EUV requires multi-beam mask writers and called Austria's IMS Nanofabrication the established leader in them. Counting all electron-beam mask writers, CSET put IMS at 46.6 percent of 2025 sales and Japan's NuFlare at 39.2 percent.

aka: mask blanks, EUV blank, EUV blanks, photomask blank, photomask blanks, blank plate, DUV blanks
plain: A mask blank is a photomask before any pattern is on it. It is a six-inch square of very flat glass carrying the film that the pattern will be cut into. For extreme ultraviolet that film sits on a mirror of about forty pairs of ultrathin layers, and a particle buried in the mirror cannot be repaired.
why: The Japanese glassmaker AGC says only three firms supply EUV blanks, and AGC and Hoya, both Japanese, are two of them. AGC spent more than a decade meeting the blank's requirements before it began mass production in 2017.

aka: physical vapor deposition, sputtering, sputtering target, sputtering targets, sputter
plain: Physical vapor deposition, or PVD, coats a wafer with metal in a vacuum. It knocks atoms off a solid slab of metal, the sputtering target, and they fly across and land on the wafer as a thin film. It lays down the metal barriers and seed layers under a chip's copper wiring.
why: Every copper wire needs that barrier, because copper seeps into the insulator around it. JX Advanced Metals puts its own share of the world market for semiconductor sputtering targets at about 65 percent as of fiscal 2026.

aka: chemical vapor deposition, PECVD, plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition, MOCVD, CVD precursor, precursor, precursors
plain: Chemical vapor deposition, or CVD, grows a film by flowing gases over a hot wafer so they react on its surface and leave a solid layer behind. The plasma-enhanced version, PECVD, runs cooler. The gases used are called precursors.
why: CVD made up $11.2 billion of a $26.2 billion deposition tool market in 2025, most of it the plasma-enhanced kind. Chinese toolmakers' share of the deposition tool market rose from 2 to 7 percent between 2019 and 2024.

aka: dielectrics, dielectric etch, dielectric properties, insulator, insulating layer
plain: A dielectric is an insulator: a material that does not conduct, such as the glassy oxides and nitrides between a chip's wires or the epoxy in a package substrate. Dielectric etch cuts holes and trenches through those insulating layers so the wires can be laid in.
why: How much signal a dielectric absorbs sets how fast a substrate or circuit board can run. So the suppliers of laminates, the insulating sheets these boards are made from, matter to AI systems.

aka: critical dimensions, CD, CD-SEM, critical-dimension, line width, line-width, line widths
plain: The critical dimension is the width of the finest printed feature on a layer. A CD-SEM is an electron microscope built to measure it across a wafer without cutting anything.
why: Fabs measure it to tell whether each lithography and etch step came out the right width. In 2025 Hitachi held 71.9 percent of the market for the tools that measure it, by CSET's count. They are the one kind of inspection or measurement tool that Japan leads.

aka: backside power, backside vias, PowerVia, Super Power Rail, backside power network
plain: Backside power delivery moves a chip's power wiring to the underside of the wafer, so the wiring above the transistors carries only signals. After the transistors and signal wiring are built, the wafer is bonded face down to a second wafer and ground thin, and the power wires are built on its back. Power arrives through tiny holes etched up from below, clear of the crowded top.
why: It is one of the few remaining ways to make a chip faster without shrinking the transistor. Intel ships it on its 18A process. TSMC says A16, its first process with it, will be production-ready in the second half of 2026.

aka: copper vias, vertical vias, vertical copper vias
plain: Vias are the small vertical holes, filled with metal, that connect one layer of wiring to the layer above or below it. A chip's wiring is full of them. An interposer has them through its whole thickness, and a package substrate has them drilled by laser through each sheet of film.
why: Every added layer brings another set of vias that can fail, so yield falls as packages and substrates grow.

aka: coater-developer, coater and developer, coater/developer track, track tool, track tools
plain: A coater/developer, or track, is the machine that spins a thin coat of photoresist onto the wafer before it enters the scanner. After the wafer comes out, the same machine washes away the exposed parts, so every printed layer passes through it twice.
why: No pattern can be printed without it. Tokyo Electron's own results put its share of the market at 91 percent in 2025.

aka: lots, wafer lot, wafer lots, per lot
plain: A lot is the batch of wafers a fab moves through its machines together, usually 25 in one sealed carrier. Recipes, inspections and yield are tracked lot by lot.
why: A fab decides how many wafers in each lot it can afford to inspect. That choice sets how much it spends on process control, the measuring that keeps each step on target.

aka: front end of line, FEOL, front-end, front-end wafers
plain: The front end of line is the first half of making a chip, the steps that build the transistors in the silicon. In the industry at large, the front end means the whole wafer fab, as against the back end where chips are packaged and tested.
why: SemiAnalysis judged in March 2026 that front-end capacity had overtaken packaging as the main bottleneck on AI chip output. But TSMC said in July 2026 that its packaging capacity still limited customers' growth.

aka: back end of line, BEOL, back-end, back-end fabs, back-end tools
plain: Inside a fab, the back end of line is the second half of making a chip, the dozen or more layers of copper wiring stacked above the transistors. In the industry at large, the back end means everything after the wafer leaves the fab: grinding, dicing, packaging and test.
why: Wiring is now as hard to make as the transistor. Among the firms that package and test chips after they leave the fab, four of the ten largest by 2024 revenue are headquartered in China, in a TrendForce ranking cited by CSET.

aka: static random-access memory, cache, on-chip memory, on-die SRAM, on-die memory, L2 cache
plain: SRAM is the fast memory built from transistors on the logic chip itself, used as a cache that holds the numbers a processor is about to need. It is far faster than the memory stacks beside the chip and holds far less.
why: The cell that holds one bit has barely shrunk since the 5 nm node, which limits how much cache a designer can afford to put on an accelerator.

aka: HVM, volume production, mass production, high volume, in volume, production ramp
plain: High-volume manufacturing is the point where a new process or product stops being a trial and is made in volume for sale. Output then climbs to full rate during the ramp.
why: Foundries announce the date a process reaches it, and before then the process makes only prototypes, as Rapidus's 2 nm line did in 2025.

aka: ramps, ramp-up, ramping, yield at ramp
plain: A ramp is the months in which a new process or product climbs from a few wafers a week to full output while the share of working chips rises. Yield is lowest at the start of the ramp and improves as engineers find which steps lose dies.
why: Whether a new process makes a profit or needs a subsidy depends on its yield in the first year.

aka: thermocompression, thermo-compression bonding, thermocompression bonder, thermocompression bonders, TCB, die bonder, die bonders, bonder, bonders
plain: Thermocompression bonding presses one die onto another, or onto a substrate, under heat and force until the tiny solder bumps between them melt and join. It is how memory dies are stacked to make high bandwidth memory (HBM) and a growing way to place chiplets on a package.
why: ASMPT says it remained the leader in these bonders in 2025, when its revenue from them rose about 146 percent. It aims for 35 to 40 percent of a market it puts at $1.6 billion in 2028.

aka: wafer dicing, dicing saw, dicing saws, grinding, wafer grinding, grinders, wafer grinders, thinning, wafer thinning
plain: Dicing cuts a finished wafer into its individual dies with a diamond saw or a laser. Grinding, done first, thins the wafer from the back, and for stacked memory it goes on until the copper columns inside the dies come through.
why: Stacked high bandwidth memory (HBM) depends on that grinding. Disco of Japan held 87 percent of the world market for dicing saws and wafer grinders in 2025, by CSET's count.

aka: panel-level, panel level packaging, rectangular panel, rectangular panels
plain: Panel-level packaging builds packages on a large rectangular sheet instead of a round wafer, so far less area is wasted at the edges and many more packages fit on one carrier. It gets around the size limits of a 300 mm wafer.
why: Powertech, a Taiwanese assembly and test firm, aims to run the first panel-level packaging line for AI chips in 2027.

aka: wafer test, probe test, wafer probe
plain: Wafer sort is the first test a chip gets, while it is still on the wafer. Thousands of needles on a probe card press onto the pads of one die, or of several dies at once, and a tester drives signals in and reads the answers. Any die that answers wrong is marked and never packaged.
why: Proving a die good before it is packaged keeps one bad die from scrapping the memory stacks and substrate it would be joined to.

aka: burn in, wafer-level burn-in, burn-in test
plain: Burn-in runs a chip hot and at raised voltage for minutes to days, so that any part that would fail early fails in the factory before it is shipped. It can run on the wafer or in the package. Aehr, a maker of burn-in systems, says its lead AI customer is moving all burn-in for its accelerators from the system level to the wafer.
why: One weak die in a package of a dozen expensive parts scraps all of them, so burn-in on the wafer protects everything else in the package.

aka: qualify, qualifies, qualified, qualifying, requalify, requalification, qualification tests, qualification lock-in
plain: Qualification is the testing a fab or a customer runs before it will accept a new material, tool or supplier. A resist, a slurry, a wafer source or a memory stack is approved for a set use, such as one layer in one fab's process, and switching means running the tests again.
why: Even a resist that passes the first time takes seven to 17 months to approve, the Semiconductor Industry Association wrote in 2023, so a second source is slow to add.

aka: second sources, second-source, multi-sourcing, dual source, single source, sole source, single-source
plain: A second source is a second supplier qualified for the same part or material, so that a fab can keep running if the first one stops shipping. A single-source part has none, and adding one means joint development and a fresh qualification.
why: When Japan put three chemicals under export licenses for South Korea in 2019, South Korea bought more from other countries. Output of all three chemicals rose at South Korean firms and at Japanese companies' affiliates in South Korea.

aka: mask shops, mask making, mask maker, mask makers
plain: A mask shop is the factory that turns a finished chip design into its set of photomasks. It writes each plate with an electron beam, inspects it and repairs it.
why: No chip can be printed until its masks are made. Chipmakers such as TSMC and SMIC run shops of their own, and independents such as Photronics sell to them and to others.

aka: silicon IP, IP blocks, licensed blocks, licensed circuit blocks, semiconductor IP, IP catalog, intellectual property
plain: In chip design, IP, short for intellectual property, means a ready-made block of circuitry, such as a processor core or a memory interface, that a design house licenses. Arm sells processor IP, and other firms sell the blocks that talk to memory, PCIe or another chiplet.
why: Each licensed block must be proven on a new process before a chip can use it. The memory interface is a demanding one, because it has to hold its timing across thousands of solder bumps into a stacked memory die.

aka: register-transfer level, register-transfer-level, register transfer level, RTL description, RTL code
plain: RTL, for register-transfer level, is the code in which a chip is first written. It is text, in a language such as SystemVerilog, that describes what every storage element holds on every tick of the clock. Software later turns it into transistors and wires.
why: It defines what the chip does. A large team checks it in simulation and emulation before tape-out, because a mistake found later needs new masks.

aka: sign-off, static timing analysis, timing signoff, timing sign-off, physical verification, signed off
plain: Signoff is the final set of automated checks a chip design must pass before tape-out. Static timing analysis checks that every signal arrives in time at the clock speed promised. Physical verification checks that every shape in the layout can be printed.
why: A foundry accepts only layouts that pass physical verification against its rules. At advanced nodes, Synopsys holds more than 90 percent of timing signoff, and Siemens more than 85 percent of physical verification.

aka: process design kit, process design kits
plain: A process design kit, or PDK, is the set of files a foundry gives designers to describe exactly what its factory can print on one process, or node. It gives the sizes, spacings and electrical behavior of every feature. Design software is checked against it before a chip is accepted.
why: Foundries develop each kit with the design-software vendors about two years before production starts and specify which tools customers must use for tape-out.

aka: RISC-V cores, RISC-V processor
