plain: RISC-V is an open instruction set, the list of basic commands a processor understands, that anyone may use without a license. Companies build their own processor cores on it, and Nvidia now uses such cores for small control tasks inside every GPU.
why: It is the license-free alternative to Arm's processor designs.

aka: PCI Express, PCIe 6, PCIe 7
plain: PCIe is the standard connector and link that joins a processor to the cards inside a computer, an accelerator included. In an AI server it carries data between the host processor and the GPUs, while faster private links join the GPUs to each other.
why: The PCIe block is licensed IP that has to be proven on each new node before a chip can use it.

aka: Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express, UCIe 3.0
plain: UCIe is an open standard for the short, very fast link between two chiplets sitting side by side in one package. It lets chiplets from different vendors be wired together, the way PCIe lets cards from different vendors share a computer.
why: Accelerators too large to print as one chip are built from chiplets, and a shared standard lets more firms supply the pieces.

aka: serializer-deserializer, high-speed serial links, serial links, serial link
plain: A SerDes, for serializer-deserializer, is the circuit at the edge of a chip that turns many slow parallel signals into one very fast stream over a single pair of wires. A SerDes at the other end turns the stream back into parallel signals. Every link out of an accelerator, to another chip, a switch or an optical module, runs through one.
why: SerDes speed sets how much data a chip can move. Many chip designers license the blocks as IP, and each design has to be proven in silicon on every new process.

aka: microbumps, solder bump, solder bumps, bumps, bump, bump metrology
plain: A microbump is a dot of solder that joins a die to the interposer or substrate beneath it. In Intel's 2.5D packages microbumps sit 36 microns apart, less than half a hair's width. Each one is an electrical connection that has to survive as the package heats and cools.
why: Their spacing limits how many connections fit between stacked or neighboring chips. Hybrid bonding, which joins copper straight to copper, would pack connections far closer, but it is not yet ready for HBM.

aka: RDL, redistribution wiring, redistribution layers
plain: A redistribution layer is a thin sheet of fine copper wiring, laid down in resin, that spreads a die's tightly spaced connections out to a wider pattern the package can handle. CoWoS-R and CoWoS-L use it in place of a full silicon interposer.
why: TSMC pushed packages past 3.3 times the reticle size by swapping silicon for redistribution wiring.

aka: silicon bridges, EMIB, silicon-bridge, local silicon bridges, embedded bridge
plain: A silicon bridge is a small sliver of silicon carrying dense wiring. It is set into the package only where two dies need thousands of connections between them, so the rest of the package can use cheaper wiring. Intel calls its version EMIB, and TSMC's CoWoS-L uses the same idea.
why: Bridges let a package grow past a single interposer's size limit, and CoWoS-L uses them to package Nvidia's Blackwell and Rubin chips. The bridges in Blackwell needed very high placement accuracy, and packaging issues limited its supply.

aka: PCB, PCBs, printed circuit boards, circuit board, circuit boards, high-multilayer PCB
plain: A printed circuit board is the flat green or black card that electronic parts are soldered onto, with its wiring etched from copper sheets and stacked in layers. Boards for AI servers can run past 30 layers.
why: It carries the power and the links between GPUs. How much signal its laminate absorbs is now a main design limit.

aka: laminates, copper-clad laminate, copper-clad laminates, low-loss laminate, core laminate
plain: A laminate is a stiff sheet made by pressing glass cloth and resin together, usually with copper foil bonded to its faces. It is the material a circuit board or a substrate core is cut from. A low-loss laminate absorbs little of the signal passing through the wires on it.
why: How much signal the laminate absorbs has become a main design limit on the boards that link GPUs.

aka: T-glass, low-expansion glass, glass fiber cloth, low-expansion glass cloth
plain: Glass cloth is a woven fabric of fine glass fibers that gives a substrate core or circuit board its stiffness. T-glass is a special grade that barely expands when heated, which helps keep a large package flat.
why: Nitto Boseki of Japan claims an overwhelming advantage in low-expansion glass cloth. It says demand seems to have risen about two to three times since its fiscal 2024 to 2027 plan was set.

aka: CTE, thermal expansion, expansion mismatch, low-CTE
plain: The coefficient of thermal expansion is how much a material expands for each degree it warms. Silicon barely expands and epoxy expands more, so when the two are bonded and heated, the package bends.
why: Warpage control, keeping a package from bending, means matching expansion across die, bridge, interposer and substrate. It gets harder as packages grow.

aka: base chip, base logic die, logic base die, HBM base die
plain: The base die is the bottom chip of an HBM stack, the one that manages the memory dies above it and talks to the processor on their behalf. For HBM4, SK hynix moved it to TSMC's advanced logic process so it can hold more functions. Samsung's HBM4, shipped from February 2026, uses a 4 nm logic base die.
why: SK hynix made its own base dies up to HBM3E, so the move gives TSMC a role inside a product it does not make.

aka: 3D NAND, NAND flash, flash memory, 128-layer NAND
plain: NAND is the memory that keeps data when the power is off. It is the storage inside a phone, a laptop drive or a data center disk. 3D NAND stacks its cells in many layers, made by etching holes far deeper than they are wide. It is slow next to DRAM and is not used inside an AI accelerator.
why: Under the October 2022 US rules, items subject to US export rules bound for a fab in China that makes NAND with 128 or more layers need a license. The proposed MATCH Act would name YMTC, a Chinese NAND maker, in the law itself.

aka: JESD270-4, JEDEC standard
plain: JEDEC is the industry body that writes the standards for memory chips, so that a memory stack from any maker fits any processor built to the same specification. Its HBM4 standard, published in April 2025, sets the width and speed of the interface.
why: Makers now ship HBM4 faster than the standard's 8 Gb/s per pin. Samsung's runs at 11.7, SK hynix's above 10 and Micron's above 11. Each customer runs its own qualification tests, so meeting the standard does not by itself win an order.

aka: bandwidth density, bandwidth-density
plain: Memory bandwidth density is how much data a memory stack can move each second divided by the area of its package or stack, in gigabytes per second per square millimeter. The December 2024 rule controls any stack above 2, and BIS said every HBM stack then in production exceeded that.
why: One threshold catches every HBM stack in production, including stacks made outside the United States, so the control reaches all three makers, SK hynix, Samsung and Micron. A license exception still lets stacks below 3.3 go straight to a chip designer's packaging site. HBM already packaged with a processor falls under the chip rules instead.

aka: baseboards, SXM, OAM, HGX, HGX baseboard
plain: A baseboard is the large circuit board that eight accelerator modules bolt onto inside a server. It carries their power and the links between them. On Nvidia's baseboard, switch chips let any two modules reach each other at full speed. Nvidia's module is called SXM and its baseboard HGX. The open-standard equivalents are OAM and UBB.
why: With an eight-module baseboard, the eight accelerators in one server work as one unit. Rack-scale systems such as the NVL72 drop the baseboard and join 72 GPUs through switch trays in the rack.

aka: Quantum-2, Quantum-X800
plain: InfiniBand is a networking standard long used in supercomputers, with low delay and no dropped packets. AI clusters relied on it to link thousands of servers before Ethernet caught up, and Nvidia still sells both.
why: The choice between InfiniBand and Ethernet decides who sells the switch chips. Broadcom has doubled the bandwidth of its Ethernet switch chips with each generation since 2019.

aka: Ultra Ethernet, Spectrum-X, Spectrum-X Ethernet, Tomahawk, Ethernet switch
plain: Ethernet is the ordinary networking standard of offices and the internet, now made fast and reliable enough to link the servers of an AI cluster. Its switch chips, such as Broadcom's Tomahawk, route traffic between thousands of accelerators.
why: Broadcom has doubled the bandwidth of its Ethernet switch chips every generation, from 25.6 Tbps on one chip in Tomahawk 4 in 2019 to 102.4 in Tomahawk 6 in 2025.

aka: co-packaged, co-packaging, CPO, plug-in modules, plug-in optics
plain: Co-packaged optics puts the parts that turn electrical signals into light and back onto the switch chip's own package instead of into plug-in modules at the front of the box. Broadcom keeps the lasers that supply the light in separate modules that can be replaced in the field.
why: Broadcom and Nvidia are moving the optics onto the switch package partly to cut the power the optics use. Broadcom says its Tomahawk 6 Davisson cuts optical interconnect power by 70 percent.

aka: InP, indium
plain: Indium phosphide is a crystal grown from the metal indium and phosphorus. It gives off light when current passes through it, which silicon cannot do efficiently. The lasers inside the fastest optical modules are made of it.
why: China produced about 70 percent of the world's indium in 2025. In February 2025 it put indium under new export restrictions and began requiring export permits for indium phosphide substrates. In March 2026 Nvidia agreed to invest $2 billion each in Coherent and Lumentum, alongside purchase commitments for their lasers.

aka: busbars, copper busbar, copper busbars
plain: A busbar is a thick bar of solid copper that carries large currents down the back of a rack to the boards that need them. An ordinary cable carrying the same current would overheat. At the 54 volts used inside racks such as the GB300 NVL72, a one-megawatt rack would need up to 200 kilograms of busbar, by Nvidia's estimate.
why: Nvidia is moving its racks to 800 volts, which cuts the current, so a megawatt rack will not need bars that heavy.

aka: power shelves, rack power shelf
plain: A power shelf is a slide-in unit in a rack that converts the incoming supply to the voltage the boards use and feeds it to the busbar. A GB300 NVL72 rack draws its 142 kilowatts through eight of them at 33 kilowatts each.
why: Many firms supply the shelves and the boards behind them. The large transformers upstream commonly took three years to arrive in 2024.

aka: large power transformers, transformer, transformers, switchgear, substation
plain: A large power transformer is a machine that changes grid electricity from one voltage to another, for example from transmission voltage down to a level a data center can use. Switchgear is the heavy switching and protection equipment around it. Together they make up the substation at the gate of the campus.
why: In 2024 lead times of 36 months were commonly quoted, against under a year before the pandemic. Of the units put into US service in 2019, 82 percent were imported.

aka: mm2, square millimeters, square millimeter
plain: mm² means square millimeters, the unit chip areas are given in. A lithography scanner prints at most 858 mm² in one shot, and each compute die in an Nvidia B200 is about 800 mm². In 2028 TSMC plans to start making chip packages whose base layer, the wiring that links the chips, covers 14 scanner shots.
why: Yield, the share of dies that work, falls as die area grows, so the cost of each working chip rises faster than its area.

aka: kW, kilowatts, megawatt, MW, megawatts, gigawatt, GW, gigawatts
plain: A kilowatt is a thousand watts. A megawatt is a thousand kilowatts, and a gigawatt a thousand megawatts, about the output of one large power station. A GB300 NVL72 rack draws up to 142 kilowatts. The largest data center campuses are planned in gigawatts.
why: AI deals are now counted in gigawatts too, as when OpenAI and Broadcom announced 10 gigawatts of accelerators. Power equipment now arrives more slowly than the chips.

aka: terawatt-hour, terawatt-hours, terawatt hours
plain: A terawatt-hour is a billion kilowatt-hours, the unit national electricity use is counted in. US data centers used 192 TWh in 2024, 4.7 percent of the country's electricity.
why: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's reference case projects 649 TWh in 2030, 11.8 percent of forecast US electricity use, within a range of 521 to 843 TWh.

aka: TB/s, Gb/s, Tbps, gigabytes per second, terabytes per second, gigabits per second, terabits per second
plain: GB/s is gigabytes per second, the measure of how much data a link or a memory can move. TB/s is a thousand times more. A lowercase b, as in Gb/s or Tbps, counts bits, each an eighth of a byte. One HBM4 stack moves over 2 TB/s. NVLink 6 gives each GPU 3,600 GB/s, according to Nvidia's January 2026 Rubin launch.
why: The October 2022 US rule caught chips with a processing score of 4,800 or more and an input and output rate of 600 GB/s or more (87 FR 62186). Since January 2026, chips with total DRAM bandwidth below 6,500 GB/s and a processing score, or TPP, below 21,000 can be licensed case by case for China (91 FR 1684).

aka: wafers a month, wafer starts, wafer starts per month, WSPM, wafer starts a month, million wafers per month
plain: Wafers per month is how fab capacity is counted: the number of wafers a plant can start through its line each month. A TSMC gigafab runs more than 100,000. In September 2025 SemiAnalysis conservatively put SMIC's capacity at 7 nm and below at 45,000 a month by the end of 2025. Figures are often converted to 8-inch or 12-inch equivalents so plants with different wafer sizes can be compared.
why: In June 2024 the industry association SEMI forecast China at 10.1 million wafers a month in 2025, the most of any region. In 2026 it projected China would stay largest through 2027, but little of that capacity is advanced.

aka: 300-millimeter, 12-inch wafer, 12-inch wafers, 12-inch equivalent, 200 mm, 8-inch, 8-inch-equivalent, 450 mm, 150 mm
plain: 300 mm is the diameter of the standard wafer, about twelve inches. Older fabs run 200 mm, or 8-inch, wafers. The last increase in wafer size, to 300 mm, came in 2002.
why: Advanced chips start on 300 mm wafers. In SEMI's November 2020 World Fab Forecast, which CSET cited in January 2021, they carried 99.7 percent of world fab capacity at 45 nm and below.

aka: nm, nanometers, microns, micrometer, micrometers, angstrom, angstroms, picometer, picometers
plain: A nanometer is a billionth of a meter. A micron, or micrometer, is a thousand nanometers, an angstrom is a tenth of a nanometer, and a picometer is a thousandth. Lithography light is measured in nanometers, package bumps in microns, and mirror flatness in picometers.
why: Node names such as 2 nm no longer describe any feature that size, but the physical limits of printing and stacking are still measured in these units.

aka: pitches, half-pitch, gate pitch, metal pitch, wire pitch, line pitch
plain: Pitch is the distance from one line on a chip to the next, center to center, so it counts the line and the gap together. Half-pitch is half that. A 16 nm pitch means lines 16 nanometers apart. The 2022 US rules set a DRAM threshold at 18 nm half-pitch.
why: Unlike a node name, pitch measures something physical on the chip. But SemiAnalysis calls a single pitch an incomplete metric for comparing processes.

aka: 5 nm-class, 7 nm-class, 2 nm-class, nanometer-class, nm class
plain: Nm-class, as in 7 nm-class, means a process roughly as dense as the foundries' 7 nm generation. The label is used when a maker's own name for the node is different.
why: China's SMIC builds its 7 nm-class processes without extreme ultraviolet machines, and its most advanced, N+3, reaches the density of TSMC's 6 nm-class process.

aka: logic density, chip density, transistors per square millimeter, density gain
plain: Transistor density is how many transistors fit in a square millimeter of chip. SemiAnalysis measured SMIC's N+3 at 113.4 million, against 107.7 million for TSMC's N6. TSMC says N2P gives 1.2 times the logic density and 1.15 times the chip density of N3E. A16, which adds backside power, gives up to 1.10 times the chip density of N2P. TSMC says A14, planned for 2028, will give more than 20 percent more logic density than N2.
why: Density sets how much logic fits on a die of a given size. No foundry publishes wafer prices, so cost per transistor cannot be worked out from public figures.

aka: wafers an hour, wafers per hour, wafers-per-hour
plain: Throughput is how many wafers a machine can process in an hour. ASML's NXE:3800E EUV scanner reaches 220.
why: Throughput sets the cost of each layer and how many lots, or batches of wafers, a fab can afford to inspect. Brighter EUV light sources and multi-beam inspection tools both aim to raise it.

aka: utilization rate, fab utilization
plain: Utilization is how full a fab's lines are running, as a share of what they could run. Most of a fab's costs, such as paying off its tools, stay the same whether it runs full or half empty, so utilization largely decides whether it makes money.
why: SMIC ran its lines 93.5 percent full in 2025, and its gross margin that year was 21 percent.

aka: operating profit, operating loss, operating income
plain: Operating margin is the share of revenue left after paying both the cost of making the product and the cost of running the company, research and sales included. It is lower than gross margin, which counts only the cost of making.
why: SK hynix's earnings release gives no gross margin, only an operating margin, which was 76 percent in the June 2026 quarter.

aka: lead times, delivery time
plain: Lead time is the wait between placing an order and receiving it. A wafer clears a leading-edge fab in months, while in 2024 a large power transformer commonly took three years.
why: Chip supply and power equipment are both constrained. Micron said in its report for the quarter to May 2026 that AI-driven memory and storage growth was outpacing industry supply. Waits for large power equipment run to years.

aka: oligopolies, duopoly, three-firm oligopoly
plain: An oligopoly is a market with only a few sellers, so each one's decisions move the price. A duopoly has two. DRAM, industrial gases, substrates and chip testers are all oligopolies.
why: The fewer the sellers, the more one accident or one license decision moves the market. With a single seller, losing that seller stops the buyer's production line.

aka: leading-edge, at the leading edge, advanced node, advanced nodes, advanced-node
plain: The leading edge is the newest generation of chipmaking process in volume production. In 2026 that means the 3 nm and 2 nm nodes, made only by TSMC, Samsung and Intel. A leading-edge chip is one built on it.
why: Gate-all-around transistors are the design used at 2 nm, and only TSMC, Intel and Samsung make them in volume. In 2024 the United States put a worldwide license requirement on the technology for building them.

aka: mature nodes, mature-node, mature logic, older nodes, older lines, trailing edge
plain: A mature node is an older chipmaking process, 28 nm and above, that has run for years and competes on price. Most of the world's wafers come off these lines, making power chips, analog parts and microcontrollers.
why: China held 33 percent of the world's logic capacity at 28 nm and above in 2022. In the five years before May 2024, Chinese companies invested $63 billion in 73 fabs, mostly for chips above 28 nm, SIA and BCG reported.

aka: original design manufacturer, ODMs, contract manufacturer, contract manufacturers, contract manufacturing, EMS, server ODM
plain: An ODM, for original design manufacturer, is a firm such as Foxconn, Quanta or Wistron that designs and builds servers and racks to a customer's specification. The customer's name goes on the box. A contract manufacturer does the assembly only.
why: More than 50 makers of systems and components were gearing up for Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack in October 2025, Nvidia said. In its filing for the quarter to July 2026, Nvidia said the complexity of producing its data center systems had caused production delays.

aka: inference chip, inference chips, inference accelerator, inference accelerators, training and inference
plain: Inference is running a finished AI model to answer requests, such as a prompt. Training, a run of weeks on a cluster of accelerators, builds the model first. To write each word of an answer, the chip reads the whole model from memory, does a little arithmetic and waits for the next read. Training reuses each number it fetches, so it fetches little and computes a lot.
why: In inference, memory size and speed usually set how many people one chip can serve.

aka: weights, frontier model weights, trained weights
plain: Model weights are the billions of numbers that make up a trained AI model. They are the file that runs on the chips, so copying the weights copies the model.
why: A chip reads the model's weights from memory for each word it writes, so bigger models need more HBM. The AI Diffusion rule also made frontier model weights a controlled item, ECCN 4E091.

aka: export controls, export licensing, export license, export licenses, export licence, export licences, export-control
plain: An export control is a rule that requires the government's permission for a sale. The government names an item and a country or a buyer. From then on its own companies must hold a license before they ship that item to that country or buyer. The United States extends some of these rules to goods made abroad with American technology.
why: It works only when the controlling country's firms make something the buyer cannot get elsewhere.

plain: 3A090 is the entry in the US export control list that covers advanced AI chips, defined by their total processing performance and performance density. Its part c, added in December 2024, covers high bandwidth memory. 4A090 covers the computers built from the chips. A chip that falls under 3A090.a needs a license for China. The AI Diffusion rule of January 2025 extended that requirement to every destination. But BIS says it enforces the requirement only for Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 and for firms headquartered in D:5 or Macau.
why: It decides which AI chips need a license for China, so designers now build chips around its thresholds.

plain: 3B001 is the main entry in the US export control list for chipmaking equipment. It is written as process specifications, such as an etch tool that cuts sideways or a deposition tool that coats holes more than 200 times deeper than they are wide. BIS created 3B090 in October 2022 and folded it into 3B001 and 3B002 in October 2023 (88 FR 73424). The related 3D and 3E entries cover the software and know-how that go with the tools.
why: It decides which chipmaking tools need an export license. It defines a tool by the process it can run, because the same chamber can add or remove material depending on its recipe.

aka: affiliates rule, 50 percent rule, affiliates of listed entities
plain: The Affiliates Rule extended the Entity List to any company anywhere in the world that is at least half owned by a listed firm. The aim was to stop a listed company from buying through a subsidiary. It took effect on 29 September 2025 and was suspended for a year six weeks later.
why: It is suspended until 9 November 2026. If it returns, subsidiaries at least half owned by listed firms will again need licenses.

aka: US persons, U.S. person, U.S. persons
plain: In export law a US person is any American citizen, permanent resident or company, wherever in the world they are, and anyone in the United States. Since October 2022 a US person may not service or support an advanced chip fab in China without a license.
why: The rule reaches people as well as goods, so American citizens, residents and companies need a license to support advanced chipmaking in China.

aka: consignees, named consignee, named consignees, ultimate consignee
plain: The consignee is the party a shipment is sent to, the name on the export license. A named consignee, such as G42 in the United Arab Emirates, can receive controlled chips on the terms attached to its own name.
why: The July 2026 UAE rule names the Emirati government, G42 and eight US-headquartered AI companies as consignees who can take controlled AI chips without a license. The license-free treatment is tied to those named buyers.

aka: approval is presumed, presumed approval
plain: A presumption of approval means a license is still required but will normally be granted. It is the opposite of a presumption of denial, and one rule can contain both. HBM license applications for Macau and Country Group D:5 are presumed approved when neither the buyer nor its ultimate parent is headquartered in either place, and presumed denied otherwise (15 CFR 742.6(b)(10)(ii)).
why: The split lets HBM reach plants in China owned by firms headquartered elsewhere while holding it back from Chinese-owned buyers.

aka: case by case, case-by-case, reviewed case by case
plain: Case-by-case review means a license is required and each application is judged on its own, with no presumption either way. Since January 2026 Nvidia's H200 and AMD's MI325X have been reviewed this way for China, with conditions attached to each approval.
why: It is the middle ground between an open market and a presumption of denial. In early 2026 the United States settled on it for chips such as the H200 bound for China.

aka: AIA, Artificial Intelligence Authorization
plain: License Exception AIA, for Artificial Intelligence Authorization, lets the top band of AI chips ship without a license to nineteen destinations. They are listed in supplement no. 5 to part 740, and the United States is among them. The AI Diffusion rule created it in January 2025 as the exception inside a worldwide license requirement.
why: BIS said in May 2025 that it would not enforce the AI Diffusion rule. But the rule was never repealed, so AIA still stands in the regulations. BIS says it enforces the worldwide requirement only for Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 and for firms headquartered in D:5 or Macau.

aka: ACM, Advanced Compute Manufacturing
plain: License Exception ACM, for Advanced Compute Manufacturing, lets controlled AI chips and related items go without a license to private-sector firms that develop, make or store them. The items must be bound for customers outside Macau and Country Group D:5. It was created alongside License Exceptions AIA and LPP.
why: It keeps the AI Diffusion rule's worldwide license requirement from catching chips that are only passing through factories and warehouses on their way to an eligible customer.

aka: AI Diffusion, diffusion rule, Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion, AI Diffusion framework
plain: The AI Diffusion rule, published on 15 January 2025, required a license to ship the most capable AI chips anywhere in the world. Its exceptions allowed unlimited shipments to nineteen destinations, capped volumes elsewhere and none to China. It also controlled the weights of frontier AI models.
why: Four months later BIS said it would not enforce the rule. But it withdrew none of the text, so the license requirement and exceptions still stand in the regulations. BIS says it enforces the requirement only for Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 and for firms headquartered in D:5 or Macau.

aka: FR, 89 FR, 91 FR, 88 FR, Federal Register notice
plain: The Federal Register is the US government's daily journal, where every new rule is published. An export rule can take effect a few days before it is printed there, as the UAE rule did in July 2026. A citation such as 89 FR 96790 means volume 89, page 96790, and is the usual way to cite a rule.
why: US export rules change by notices published there, with no act of Congress needed.

aka: CFR, Code of Federal Regulations, 15 CFR 742.6, part 742, part 740, part 734, supplement no. 5 to part 740, supplement no. 5
plain: The Code of Federal Regulations is the standing text of US rules, sorted into titles and parts. Title 15 holds the Export Administration Regulations. Part 734 says what is subject to them. Part 740 lists the license exceptions, and its supplement no. 5 lists the nineteen destinations eligible for License Exception AIA. Part 742 sets the licensing policy for each control.
why: A rule announced in the Federal Register stays in the CFR until it is removed, so the unenforced AI Diffusion rule still stands in the regulations.

aka: Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry
plain: METI is Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, the ministry that writes Japan's export controls and funds its chip industry. It put advanced chipmaking equipment under export license from July 2023. It also supports the chipmaker Rapidus and new capacity for mask blanks, the glass plates that photomasks are made from.
why: Japan's controls apply to every destination and name no country, and METI decides them.

aka: Ministry of Commerce, China's Ministry of Commerce
plain: MOFCOM is China's Ministry of Commerce, the ministry that writes and administers China's own export controls. Its notices put gallium, germanium and seven rare earths under license. In December 2024 it banned exports of gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials to the United States.
why: China's retaliation targets inputs such as these minerals, and MOFCOM signs each notice.

aka: CHIPS and Science Act, CHIPS incentives, CHIPS money, CHIPS Act grants, CHIPS authorization, CHIPS Act support, CHIPS award
plain: The CHIPS and Science Act authorized about $52.7 billion of US federal money for the chip industry. By July 2025 the Commerce Department had awarded $30.9 billion of direct funding to 19 companies for 40 projects.
why: Its grants paid a median 14.2 percent of each funded project's capital cost. In August 2025, $5.7 billion of grants awarded to Intel but not yet paid went into the government's $8.9 billion purchase of a 9.9 percent stake in Intel.

aka: National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund, National Integrated Circuit Fund, third chip fund, China's third chip fund
plain: The Big Fund is the nickname for China's National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund, the state vehicle that puts government money into Chinese chip firms. Its third round, raised in May 2024, came to 344 billion yuan, about $47 billion.
why: CSIS puts China's cumulative state funding for chips since 2014 at an estimated $150 billion. The money has built a domestic tool industry but no leading-edge node.

aka: Macao, China or Macau, China and Macau
plain: Macau is a Chinese city with its own customs territory, like Hong Kong, so goods can enter it under separate rules. US export controls name China and Macau together to close that route, and treat a firm headquartered in either the same way.
why: Under the US rules on advanced AI chips, a chip that needs a license for China needs one for Macau too.

aka: specialty gas, electronic specialty gases, bulk gases, bulk gas, electronic gases, process gas, process gases
plain: Specialty gases are the gases a fab uses in small amounts, each for one job. Silane, for example, carries silicon into the chamber to build a film, and nitrogen trifluoride cleans the chamber. They arrive in cylinders. Bulk gases, such as nitrogen and oxygen, come by pipeline or from plants built at the fab.
why: Specialty gases are shipped to the fab in cylinders, so a government or a war can cut them off. Ukraine supplied about 70 percent of the world's neon before Russia invaded in 2022.

aka: hydrofluoric acid, HF, ultra-high-purity hydrofluoric acid, high-purity hydrogen fluoride
plain: Hydrogen fluoride is a gas that dissolves glass, and hydrofluoric acid is its solution in water. Fabs use both to strip oxide layers and clean wafers between steps. Like other cleaning chemicals, it is purified until metal impurities are down to parts per trillion.
why: When Japan put it under individual export licenses for South Korea in 2019, Japan's exports of it to South Korea fell 87.9 percent. South Korea bought more from the United States and Taiwan and made more at home.

aka: NF3
plain: Nitrogen trifluoride is a gas that cleans process chambers between wafers. Split apart in a plasma, it releases fluorine that scours the deposits off the inside of the chamber.
why: A shortage of any one chemical can stop a fab. SK Specialty of South Korea has made nitrogen trifluoride since 2001, when it became the first company to produce the gas there.

aka: neon gas, semiconductor-grade neon
plain: Neon, mixed with krypton or argon and fluorine, is the gas inside the lasers that give deep ultraviolet scanners their light. A fab uses it by the cylinder, and those scanners cannot print without it.
why: Ukraine supplied about 70 percent of the world's neon before Russia invaded in 2022. Many chipmakers had added to their gas stockpiles after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, and several reported adequate supplies from China.

aka: wet chemical, wet processing, wet clean, cleaning chemicals, process chemicals
plain: Wet chemicals are the liquids a wafer is dipped in or sprayed with between steps: acids that strip a layer, solvents that remove resist, and ultrapure water rinses. Wet processing is any step done in liquid.
why: CSET's January 2021 brief, drawing on 2019 market reports, put five firms at more than 60 percent of the wet chemicals market. BIS controls wet processing tools by how selectively they etch one material over another.

aka: gallium, germanium, antimony
plain: Gallium and germanium are metals used in electronics. Gallium goes into compound chips such as radio parts, LEDs and lasers, and germanium into fiber optics, infrared optics, semiconductors and solar cells. Both are recovered as byproducts, gallium from processing bauxite and germanium from certain zinc ores and coal.
why: The US Geological Survey put China's share of world production of primary low-purity gallium at 99 percent in February 2026. China has required licenses to export both metals since August 2023. Its December 2024 ban on exports of both to the United States is suspended until 27 November 2026.

aka: rare earth, rare-earth, rare earth elements, medium and heavy rare earths
plain: The rare earths are a group of metals, including samarium and yttrium, that go into the strong magnets in motors, disk drives and wind turbines, and into some lasers and glass.
why: Beijing put seven of them under export license in April 2025. In October 2025 it claimed jurisdiction over foreign goods containing Chinese rare earths worth 0.1 percent or more of their value. That rule is suspended until 10 November 2026.

aka: metal-oxide resists, metal oxide resist, tin-oxide resist, metal-oxide EUV photoresist
plain: A metal-oxide resist is a photoresist built on clusters with a tin-oxide core. It absorbs more extreme ultraviolet light than a chemically amplified resist. That helps because an EUV dose arrives as relatively few photons.
why: Resist makers aim it at High-NA tools and the tightest pitches. The Japanese resist maker JSR agreed in 2021 to buy Inpria, an Oregon maker of these resists. In 2024 a company owned by a Japanese state-backed fund took 84.36 percent of JSR.

aka: HPC, HPC platform, high-performance computers
plain: High-performance computing is the industry's name for the heavy end of the market: supercomputers, AI accelerators and the server processors beside them. A foundry's HPC platform is the version of a node tuned for those chips.
why: AI accelerators are part of this segment and need package substrates with more layers than earlier HPC chips. Ajinomoto, which makes the insulating film between those layers, counts 11 layers of it on each side of the core in a 2026 AI package substrate, against nine on each side of an HPC substrate around 2023.

aka: chips, microchip, microchips, semiconductor chip
plain: A chip is a small rectangle of silicon, usually smaller than a fingernail, that carries a complete electronic circuit, often made of billions of transistors. It is cut from a wafer after the circuit has been built up on it layer by layer.
why: The supply chain is every firm and country that takes part in making chips, and some of them can stop production.

aka: MR-MUF, Advanced MR-MUF, TC-NCF bonding
plain: TC-NCF and MR-MUF are two ways of joining the thinned memory chips in an HBM stack. In TC-NCF, thermocompression with non-conductive film, each chip is pressed onto the one below under heat, with a thin insulating film between them. Samsung uses it for its twelve-high HBM3E. In MR-MUF, used by SK hynix, the chips are stacked first, and a liquid protective material is injected between them and hardened.
why: Thinner chips and taller stacks warp more easily, and both methods aim to control that. SK hynix says its Advanced MR-MUF also dissipates heat well.
